nameStory: The 'medicinalis' in this spider's scientific name means 'medicinal' in Latin, though there's no evidence this funnel weaver was ever used for healing purposes. This naming likely reflects the historical tendency of early naturalists to assign medicinal-sounding names to newly discovered species, perhaps hoping they might possess useful properties.
description: Coras medicinalis is a funnel weaver spider that builds distinctive sheet webs with funnel-shaped retreats. Like other members of its family, it has a brownish body with long, sturdy legs that help it dash across its web to capture prey. These spiders are moderately sized and blend well with bark and leaf litter where they typically construct their webs. They're part of a larger group of funnel weavers found throughout North America.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates a flat sheet web with a distinctive funnel-shaped tube retreat at one corner, often built against tree bark or in rock crevices where the silky sheet feels smooth but not sticky to the touch

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Has the typical funnel weaver build with a somewhat elongated abdomen and relatively long, sturdy legs that appear well-suited for running across web surfaces

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Sits at the mouth of its funnel retreat and darts out lightning-fast when prey lands on the web sheet, then quickly drags the victim back into the funnel

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Displays brownish coloration with subtle patterns that help it blend with bark and natural debris, though specific markings can vary between individuals

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Has eight eyes arranged in two rows like other funnel weavers, though you'll need to get quite close to see this arrangement clearly

habitat: Look for Coras medicinalis in wooded areas where it can anchor its funnel webs to tree bark, fallen logs, or rocky outcrops. These spiders prefer locations that offer both solid attachment points for their webs and natural crevices where they can extend their funnel retreats. They're often found in mixed deciduous and coniferous forests throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging and rebuilding webs after winter. Look for fresh, clean sheet webs appearing on tree trunks and rocks.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most obvious and spiders are actively hunting. This is the best time to observe their lightning-fast prey capture behavior.
seasonality.fall: Mating season occurs and egg sacs may be produced. Webs might appear more worn but spiders remain active until cold weather.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, with the species overwintering in immature stages or as eggs, though some adults may survive mild winters in protected locations.

funFact: Funnel weaver spiders like Coras medicinalis can run across their webs at speeds of up to 1.7 feet per second - that's like a human sprinting at 70 miles per hour relative to body size!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Coras species and funnel weavers, but the web structure is more diagnostic than the spider itself. Remember: if you see a flat sheet web with a funnel retreat (not a classic orb web), you're looking at a funnel weaver rather than the more familiar garden spiders.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'funnel weavers,' these spiders don't actually weave their webs in the traditional sense - they lay down sheets of silk and modify them into funnel shapes. The term 'weaver' is somewhat misleading compared to orb weavers who create intricate circular patterns.
compareHints: Distinguishing Coras medicinalis from its close relatives like Coras lamellosus or the Northern Spurred Woodland Funnelweaver requires examining fine details of body structure that are difficult to see in the field. For practical identification, focus on the characteristic funnel web structure and habitat preferences rather than trying to separate individual Coras species. All create similar sheet webs with funnel retreats and have comparable brownish coloration.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Distinguishing between different Coras species requires close examination of anatomical features that are difficult to see in the field.

The Northern Spurred Woodland Funnelweaver can be distinguished from its Coras relatives primarily by the male's distinctive leg spurs and its preference for higher elevation, cooler woodland habitats.
Distinguishing Coras juvenilis from its close relatives like Coras medicinalis or Coras montanus requires expert examination of reproductive structures and other microscopic features.
Coras aerialis is virtually indistinguishable in the field from its relatives like Coras medicinalis and Coras montanus without examining reproductive structures under magnification.
